# Bounded Contexts: Relationships and Integration

## Relationships Between Contexts

The article states that "Bounded Contexts have both unrelated concepts (such as a support ticket only existing in a customer support context) but also share concepts (such as products and customers)."

Regarding mapping between contexts with overlapping concepts, Martin Fowler explains: "Different contexts may have completely different models of common concepts with mechanisms to map between these polysemic concepts for integration."

## Boundary Factors

The piece identifies what shapes these divisions: "Usually the dominant one is human culture, since models act as Ubiquitous Language, you need a different model when the language changes."

## Strategic Design

The text notes that "DDD's strategic design goes on to describe a variety of ways that you have relationships between Bounded Contexts. It's usually worthwhile to depict these using a context map."

## Cross-Context Challenges

A practical example illustrates the problem: at an electricity utility, "the word 'meter' meant subtly different things to different parts of the organization," showing how shared domain concepts create friction across team boundaries without clear context delineation.

# Product-Mode vs Project-Mode: Key Definitions

## What is Product-Mode?

**Funding & Organization:**
"A team gets funded" on a rolling basis rather than "a pre-defined solution or outstanding scope gets funded," according to the article's comparison table.

"Teams are funded to work on a particular business problem or offering over a period of time; with the nature work being defined by a business problem to address rather than a set of functions to deliver."

**Lifecycle Coverage:**
Product-mode provides funding "for building, running and iterating on the solution or even pivoting to a different solution till the underlying problem is _verifiably_ solved."

**Team Duration:**
Teams last "as long as the roadmap has business relevance. Typically, several years," contrasting sharply with project teams.

## Business Capability Alignment

"Products-mode works best when teams are organized to be simultaneously aligned with business relevant capabilities and with enterprise architecture boundaries."

The retirement calculator example demonstrates this: teams are structured around customer journey stages like "enrol employees" and "save for retirement" rather than functional areas.

## Cross-Team Features & Dependencies

"For initiatives that cut across multiple product-mode teams, it is recommended to appoint silo-penetrating, priority-negotiating, dependency-managing solution champions who work with product owners and business stakeholders."

## Roadmap & Prioritization

"Roadmap items are prioritized by product owners and their business counterparts. Cross-cutting initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership."

A practical guideline suggests "two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work" for balanced capacity allocation.

# Team Topologies: Key Definitions

## Four Team Types

**Stream-aligned team:** "aligned to a flow of work from (usually) a segment of the business domain"

**Platform team:** "a grouping of other team types that provide a compelling internal product to accelerate delivery by Stream-aligned teams"

**Enabling team:** "helps a Stream-aligned team to overcome obstacles. Also detects missing capabilities."

**Complicated Subsystem team:** "where significant mathematics/calculation/technical expertise is needed"

## Three Interaction Modes

**Collaboration:** "working together for a defined period of time to discover new things (APIs, practices, technologies, etc.)"

**X-as-a-Service:** "one team provides and one team consumes something 'as a Service'"

**Facilitation:** "one team helps and mentors another team"

## Core Concepts

**Cognitive Load:** Teams have limited mental bandwidth. The approach emphasizes "Respect Cognitive Limits" and monitoring "unnecessary complexity" to maintain team effectiveness.

**Flow of Change:** The diagram shows "Stream-aligned teams own an entire slice of the business domain...end-to-end. The Stream-aligned teams are 'You Built It, You Run It' teams."

**Team-First Design:** The methodology prioritizes understanding "how real work happens and flows" before designing organizational structures.

The term saga is commonly used in discussions of CQRS to refer to a piece of code that coordinates and routes messages between bounded contexts and aggregates, though the term process manager is preferred to refer to this type of code artifact.

You would typically expect to see a process manager routing messages between aggregates within a bounded context, and a saga managing a long-running business process that spans multiple bounded contexts.

A process manager is a class which, based on some events (that can be in multiple bounded contexts) automatically triggers an action in the system.

## Compensating Transactions

The saga concept removes the need for a distributed transaction by ensuring that each step has a defined compensating transaction, allowing the system to execute compensating transactions if an error occurs, which undoes the work completed and maintains consistency.

## Spotify's Squad Model and Cross-Team Collaboration

The Spotify model emerged from a series of blog posts and videos published in 2012 describing how Spotify organised its engineering teams. The model centres on four structural elements: Squads (small, autonomous, cross-functional teams similar to Scrum teams), Tribes (collections of squads working in related areas), Chapters (groups of people with similar skills across squads, led by a chapter lead who also serves as their line manager), and Guilds (informal communities of interest that span the entire organisation).

## Challenges with Cross-Squad Feature Delivery

While the squad model was designed for autonomy, many of these problems required cross-squad collaboration, and cross-tribe collaboration was harder than the model anticipated. The culture that made it work was not transferable.

More recently, multiple employee reviews mention coordination challenges as a consistent friction point — particularly for projects that span multiple product areas. Additionally, as squad count grows, introduce programme management as a dedicated function. Programme managers coordinate cross-squad initiatives, facilitate dependency management, and structure collaboration at scale.

The search results emphasize that while the Spotify model has been influential, Spotify has evolved since then and has stated publicly that it does not follow a fixed "Spotify Model."

## Big Picture EventStorming and Bounded Contexts

The Big Picture EventStorming helps to identify Bounded Contexts together with the dev team: Units of homogenous language and model consistency, which together form a heterogeneous whole. ## Heuristics for Identifying Bounded Context Boundaries

Brandolini provides several heuristics for determining bounded contexts:

1. **Pivotal Events**: Pivotal events mark "important" points in time, where something significant happens in the domain. These pivotal events are a good starting point to identify bounded contexts, as they often mark the boundaries between them.

# Bounded Context in Domain-Driven Design

Bounded Context represents a foundational pattern within Domain-Driven Design (DDD) that addresses the challenge of managing large, complex software systems. According to Martin Fowler's explanation, this pattern focuses on "dealing with large models and teams" by partitioning extensive models into distinct contexts while clarifying how they interact.

## The Core Problem

Large organizations frequently encounter terminology inconsistencies across different departments. Fowler illustrates this through a practical example: "the word 'meter' meant subtly different things to different parts of the organization" at an electricity utility. Such polysemic terms—words with multiple meanings—create significant challenges in software design where precision is essential.

Rather than attempting the traditional approach of building a single unified model for an entire business, DDD acknowledges that "total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective."

## How Bounded Contexts Work

Each context maintains its own unified model and Ubiquitous Language. While contexts may share common concepts like customers or products, they represent these concepts differently according to their specific needs. Mapping mechanisms enable integration between these divergent models.

Boundaries typically follow human cultural divisions, since models serve as communication tools between developers and domain experts. The strategic design section of DDD explores various relationship patterns between contexts, often visualized through context maps.

[![Order Paperback](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/JJ591569.download-paperback(en-us,PandP.10).png)](http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/1621140164/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=utf8&camp=1789&creative=9325&creativeasin=1621140164&linkcode=as2&tag=drgrimel-20) | #### Process Managers, Coordinating Workflows, and Sagas # Clarifying the terminology The term *saga* is commonly used in discussions of CQRS to refer to a piece of code that coordinates and routes messages between bounded contexts and aggregates. However, for the purposes of this guidance we prefer to use the term *process manager* to refer to this type of code artifact. There are two reasons for this: - There is a well-known, pre-existing definition of the term *saga* that has a different meaning from the one generally understood in relation to CQRS. - The term *process manager* is a better description of the role performed by this type of code artifact. Although the term saga is often used in the context of the CQRS pattern, it has a pre-existing definition. We have chosen to use the term process manager in this guidance to avoid confusion with this pre-existing definition. The term saga, in relation to distributed systems, was originally defined in the paper "[Sagas](http://www.cs.cornell.edu/andru/cs711/2002fa/reading/sagas.pdf)" by Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem. This paper proposes a mechanism that it calls a saga as an alternative to using a distributed transaction for managing a long-running business process. The paper recognizes that business processes are often comprised of multiple steps, each of which involves a transaction, and that overall consistency can be achieved by grouping these individual transactions into a distributed transaction. However, in long-running business processes, using distributed transactions can impact on the performance and concurrency of the system because of the locks that must be held for the duration of the distributed transaction. Note The saga concept removes the need for a distributed transaction by ensuring that the transaction at each step of the business process has a defined compensating transaction. In this way, if the business process encounters an error condition and is unable to continue, it can execute the compensating transactions for the steps that have already completed. This undoes the work completed so far in the business process and maintains the consistency of the system. Although we have chosen to use the term process manager, sagas may still have a part to play in a system that implements the CQRS pattern in some of its bounded contexts. Typically, you would expect to see a process manager routing messages between aggregates within a bounded context, and you would expect to see a saga managing a long-running business process that spans multiple bounded contexts. The following section describes what we mean by the term process manager. This is the working definition we used during our CQRS journey project. Note For a time the team developing the Reference Implementation used the term coordinating workflow before settling on the term process manager. This pattern is described in the book "Enterprise Integration Patterns" by Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf. # Process Manager This section outlines our definition of the term process manager. Before describing the process manager there is a brief recap of how CQRS typically uses messages to communicate between aggregates and bounded contexts. ## Messages and CQRS When you implement the CQRS pattern, you typically think about two types of message to exchange information within your system: commands and events. Commands are imperatives; they are requests for the system to perform a task or action. For example, "book two places on conference X" or "allocate speaker Y to room Z." Commands are usually processed just once, by a single recipient. Events are notifications; they inform interested parties that something has happened. For example, "the payment was rejected" or "seat type X was created." Notice how they use the past tense. Events are published and may have multiple subscribers. Typically, commands are sent within a bounded context. Events may have subscribers in the same bounded context as where they are published, or in other bounded contexts. The chapter, "[A CQRS and ES Deep Dive](jj591577%28v=pandp.10%29)" in this Reference Guide describes the differences between these two message types in detail. ## What is a process manager? In a complex system that you have modeled using aggregates and bounded contexts, there may be some business processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in multiple bounded contexts. In these business processes multiple messages of different types are exchanged by the participating aggregates. For example, in a conference management system, the business process of purchasing seats at a conference might involve an order aggregate, a reservation aggregate, and a payment aggregate. They must all cooperate to enable a customer to complete a purchase. Figure 1 shows a simplified view of the messages that these aggregates might exchange to complete an order. The numbers identify the message sequence. Note This does not illustrate how the Reference Implementation processes orders. [![Follow link to expand image](images/jj591569.1a64427f05a80c86a67d085eec52b0c5-thumb(en-us,pandp.10).png)](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/jj591569.1a64427f05a80c86a67d085eec52b0c5%28en-us,pandp.10%29.png) **Figure 1** Order processing without using a process manager In the example shown in Figure 1, each aggregate sends the appropriate command to the aggregate that performs the next step in the process. The **Order** aggregate first sends a **MakeReservation** command to the **Reservation** aggregate to reserve the seats requested by the customer. After the seats have been reserved, the **Reservation** aggregate raises a **SeatsReserved** event to notify the **Order** aggregate, and the **Order** aggregate sends a **MakePayment** command to the **Payment** aggregate. If the payment is successful, the **Order** aggregate raises an **OrderConfirmed** event to notify the **Reservation** aggregate that it can confirm the seat reservation, and the customer that the order is now complete. [![Follow link to expand image](images/jj591569.2fda46e1b448e51dd86e6891386a36dc-thumb(en-us,pandp.10).png)](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/jj591569.2fda46e1b448e51dd86e6891386a36dc%28en-us,pandp.10%29.png) **Figure 2** Order processing with a process manager The example shown in Figure 2 illustrates the same business process as that shown in Figure 1, but this time using a process manager. Now, instead of each aggregate sending messages directly to other aggregates, the messages are mediated by the process manager. This appears to complicate the process: there is an additional object (the process manager) and a few more messages. However, there are benefits to this approach. Firstly, the aggregates no longer need to know what is the next step in the process. Originally, the **Order** aggregate needed to know that after making a reservation it should try to make a payment by sending a message to the **Payment** aggregate. Now, it simply needs to report that an order has been created. Secondly, the definition of the message flow is now located in a single place, the process manager, rather than being scattered throughout the aggregates. In a simple business process such as the one shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2, these benefits are marginal. However, if you have a business process that involves six aggregates and tens of messages, the benefits become more apparent. This is especially true if this is a volatile part of the system where there are frequent changes to the business process: in this scenario, the changes are likely to be localized to a limited number of objects. In Figure 3, to illustrate this point, we introduce wait listing to the process. If some of the seats requested by the customer cannot be reserved, the system adds these seat requests to a waitlist. To make this change, we modify the **Reservation** aggregate to raise a **SeatsNotReserved** event to report how many seats could not be reserved in addition to the **SeatsReserved** event that reports how many seats could be reserved. The process manager can then send a command to the **WaitList** aggregate to waitlist the unfulfilled part of the request. [![Follow link to expand image](images/jj591569.cd1086a397727a80a919da87626af940-thumb(en-us,pandp.10).png)](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/jj591569.cd1086a397727a80a919da87626af940%28en-us,pandp.10%29.png) **Figure 3** Order processing with a process manager and a waitlist It's important to note that the process manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes messages, and in some cases translates between message types. For example, when it receives a **SeatsNotReserved** event, it sends an **AddToWaitList** command. ## When should I use a process manager? There are two key reasons to use a process manager: - When your bounded context uses a large number of events and commands that would be difficult to manage as a collection point-to-point interactions between aggregates. - When you want to make it easier to modify message routing in the bounded context. A process manager gives a single place where the routing is defined. ## When should I not use a process manager? The following list identifies reasons not to use a process manager: - You should not use a Process manager if your bounded context contains a small number of aggregate types that use a limited number of messages. - You should not use a process manager to implement any business logic in your domain. Business logic belongs in the aggregate types. ## Sagas and CQRS Although we have chosen to use the term process manager as defined earlier in this chapter, sagas may still have a part to play in a system that implements the CQRS pattern in some of its bounded contexts. Typically, you would expect to see a process manager routing messages between aggregates within a bounded context, and you would expect to see a saga managing a long-running business process that spans multiple bounded contexts. Note For a time the team developing the Reference Implementation used the term coordinating workflow before settling on the term process manager. This pattern is described in the book "Enterprise Integration Patterns" by Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf. # Process Manager This section outlines our definition of the term process manager. Before describing the process manager there is a brief recap of how CQRS typically uses messages to communicate between aggregates and bounded contexts. ## Messages and CQRS When you implement the CQRS pattern, you typically think about two types of message to exchange information within your system: commands and events. Commands are imperatives; they are requests for the system to perform a task or action. For example, "book two places on conference X" or "allocate speaker Y to room Z." Commands are usually processed just once, by a single recipient. Events are notifications; they inform interested parties that something has happened. For example, "the payment was rejected" or "seat type X was created." Notice how they use the past tense. Events are published and may have multiple subscribers. Typically, commands are sent within a bounded context. Events may have subscribers in the same bounded context as where they are published, or in other bounded contexts. The chapter, "[A CQRS and ES Deep Dive](jj591577%28v=pandp.10%29)" in this Reference Guide describes the differences between these two message types in detail. ## What is a process manager? In a complex system that you have modeled using aggregates and bounded contexts, there may be some business processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in multiple bounded contexts. In these business processes multiple messages of different types are exchanged by the participating aggregates. For example, in a conference management system, the business process of purchasing seats at a conference might involve an order aggregate, a reservation aggregate, and a payment aggregate. They must all cooperate to enable a customer to complete a purchase. Figure 1 shows a simplified view of the messages that these aggregates might exchange to complete an order. The numbers identify the message sequence. Note This does not illustrate how the Reference Implementation processes orders. [![Follow link to expand image](images/jj591569.1a64427f05a80c86a67d085eec52b0c5-thumb(en-us,pandp.10).png)](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/jj591569.1a64427f05a80c86a67d085eec52b0c5%28en-us,pandp.10%29.png) **Figure 1** Order processing without using a process manager In the example shown in Figure 1, each aggregate sends the appropriate command to the aggregate that performs the next step in the process. The **Order** aggregate first sends a **MakeReservation** command to the **Reservation** aggregate to reserve the seats requested by the customer. After the seats have been reserved, the **Reservation** aggregate raises a **SeatsReserved** event to notify the **Order** aggregate, and the **Order** aggregate sends a **MakePayment** command to the **Payment** aggregate. If the payment is successful, the **Order** aggregate raises an **OrderConfirmed** event to notify the **Reservation** aggregate that it can confirm the seat reservation, and the customer that the order is now complete. [![Follow link to expand image](images/jj591569.2fda46e1b448e51dd86e6891386a36dc-thumb(en-us,pandp.10).png)](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/jj591569.2fda46e1b448e51dd86e6891386a36dc%28en-us,pandp.10%29.png) **Figure 2** Order processing with a process manager The example shown in Figure 2 illustrates the same business process as that shown in Figure 1, but this time using a process manager. Now, instead of each aggregate sending messages directly to other aggregates, the messages are mediated by the process manager. This appears to complicate the process: there is an additional object (the process manager) and a few more messages. However, there are benefits to this approach. Firstly, the aggregates no longer need to know what is the next step in the process. Originally, the **Order** aggregate needed to know that after making a reservation it should try to make a payment by sending a message to the **Payment** aggregate. Now, it simply needs to report that an order has been created. Secondly, the definition of the message flow is now located in a single place, the process manager, rather than being scattered throughout the aggregates. In a simple business process such as the one shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2, these benefits are marginal. However, if you have a business process that involves six aggregates and tens of messages, the benefits become more apparent. This is especially true if this is a volatile part of the system where there are frequent changes to the business process: in this scenario, the changes are likely to be localized to a limited number of objects. In Figure 3, to illustrate this point, we introduce wait listing to the process. If some of the seats requested by the customer cannot be reserved, the system adds these seat requests to a waitlist. To make this change, we modify the **Reservation** aggregate to raise a **SeatsNotReserved** event to report how many seats could not be reserved in addition to the **SeatsReserved** event that reports how many seats could be reserved. The process manager can then send a command to the **WaitList** aggregate to waitlist the unfulfilled part of the request. [![Follow link to expand image](images/jj591569.cd1086a397727a80a919da87626af940-thumb(en-us,pandp.10).png)](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/jj591569.cd1086a397727a80a919da87626af940%28en-us,pandp.10%29.png) **Figure 3** Order processing with a process manager and a waitlist It's important to note that the process manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes messages, and in some cases translates between message types. For example, when it receives a **SeatsNotReserved** event, it sends an **AddToWaitList** command. ## When should I use a process manager? There are two key reasons to use a process manager: - When your bounded context uses a large number of events and commands that would be difficult to manage as a collection point-to-point interactions between aggregates. - When you want to make it easier to modify message routing in the bounded context. A process manager gives a single place where the routing is defined. ## When should I not use a process manager? The following list identifies reasons not to use a process manager: - You should not use a Process manager if your bounded context contains a small number of aggregate types that use a limited number of messages. - You should not use a process manager to implement any business logic in your domain. Business logic belongs in the aggregate types. ## Sagas and CQRS Although we have chosen to use the term process manager as defined earlier in this chapter, sagas may still have a part to play in a system that implements the CQRS pattern in some of its bounded contexts. Typically, you would expect to see a process manager routing messages between aggregates within a bounded context, and you would expect to see a saga managing a long-running business process that spans multiple bounded contexts. # Domain-Driven Design Pattern Definitions

**Bounded Context**
"Explicitly define the context within which a model applies. Explicitly set boundaries in terms of team organization, usage within specific parts of the application, and physical manifestations such as code bases and database schemas."

**Context Map**
"Identify each model in play on the project and define its bounded context. Name each bounded context, and make the names part of the ubiquitous language. Describe the points of contact between the models, outlining explicit translation for any communication."

**Continuous Integration**
"Institute a process of merging all code and other implementation artifacts frequently, with automated tests to flag fragmentation quickly. Relentlessly exercise the ubiquitous language to hammer out a shared view of the model as the concepts evolve."

**Partnership**
"Where development failure in either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both, forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts. Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and joint management of integration."

**Customer/Supplier Development**
"Establish a clear customer/supplier relationship between the two teams, meaning downstream priorities factor into upstream planning. Negotiate and budget tasks for downstream requirements so that everyone understands the commitment and schedule."

**Conformist**
"Eliminate the complexity of translation between bounded contexts by slavishly adhering to the model of the upstream team. Although this cramps the style of the downstream designers, choosing conformity enormously simplifies integration."

**Anticorruption Layer**
"As a downstream client, create an isolating layer to provide your system with functionality of the upstream system in terms of your own domain model. This layer talks to the other system through its existing interface, requiring little or no modification."

**Open-host Service**
"Define a protocol that gives access to your subsystem as a set of services. Open the protocol so that all who need to integrate with you can use it. Enhance and expand the protocol to handle new integration requirements."

**Published Language**
"Use a well-documented shared language that can express the necessary domain information as a common medium of communication, translating as necessary into and out of that language."

**Big Ball of Mud**
"Draw a boundary around the entire mess and designate it a big ball of mud. Do not try to apply sophisticated modeling within this context. Be alert to the tendency for such systems to sprawl into other contexts."

**Separate Ways**
"Declare a bounded context to have no connection to the others at all, allowing developers to find simple, specialized solutions within this small scope."

# Team Boundaries: Key Concepts from INNOQ

**Author:** Michael Plöd, Fellow at INNOQ

## Eight Key Passages on Identifying Team Boundaries

1. **Fracture Planes Definition:**
"A fracture plane is a natural seam in the software system that allows the system to be easily split into two or more parts." — Team Topologies

2. **Bounded Contexts as Primary Strategy:**
"Bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying boundaries for teams in the team topology environment."

3. **Core Challenge:**
The difficulty involves "finding appropriate boundaries for the areas of responsibility of these teams" within autonomous, cross-functional team structures.

4. **Bounded Context Purpose:**
A bounded context represents "a boundary around a (technical) model that is expressed in a consistent language and tailored to a specific purpose."

5. **Fracture Plane Combination:**
"Team Topologies explicitly stipulates a combination of fracture planes and encourages observing the section of a team from the perspective of different fracture planes."

6. **Event Storming Application:**
"A pivotal event lies at the boundary of a bounded context (or a subdomain)" while "swimlanes can be drivers for splitting bounded context candidates."

7. **Independent Service Heuristics Role:**
These techniques "cover many typical situations in modern software, but not all" and serve as a "framework for thinking."

8. **Implementation Wisdom:**
"You should proceed cautiously and avoid a complete reorganization every quarter" when adjusting team divisions.

Based on the article, here are key passages from Vernon's perspective:

**On Bounded Contexts and Microservices:**
1. "one service per bounded context" - Vernon's recommended starting point for microservice architecture.

2. "one service and one bounded context should be one deployable unit" - His guidance on alignment between services and domain boundaries.

**On Monoliths and Domain Models:**
3. "multiple domain models becoming entagled within the monolith" - Vernon identifies this as a critical problem causing systems to deteriorate.

4. "impossible to logically reason about the models together with the business and domain experts" - The consequence when distinct models get mixed together.

**On Sizing Microservices:**
5. "modelling microservices in a bounded context determined in size by the ubiquitous language" - Vernon's prescriptive approach rather than arbitrary metrics.

6. "their cohesiveness and collaboration means they should be kept together within one service" - His reasoning against splitting bounded contexts prematurely.

**On Domain Events:**
7. "publishing the events for eventual use of other microservices" - How event-driven architecture enables cross-service communication.

**On Organizational Evolution:**
8. "With experience though, they may become more fine granular, creating more microservices and deployable units" - Vernon acknowledges gradual refinement based on scaling needs.

"A bounded context is effectively a way of us modeling these kinds of groups of functionality within a domain model so from the outside the bounded contexts allows you to kind of access some sort of higher level concepts"

"If you have a series of webpages each page can be served up from different microservices, it's a very easy decompositional look because then you're effectively using URL routing as a way of dispatching requests"

"Having an explicit schema allows you to be really clear...gives you clarity for consumers of your microservices as to the structure"

"Looking at where your boundaries of your architecture without looking at the boundaries of your organization would be a bit crazy."

## 8. Independent Deployability Foundation
"Microservices really fundamentally as being a modular architecture, albeit a modular architecture with the complexity of a distributed system."

# Big Picture EventStorming: Key Concepts

## EventStorming Overview
"EventStorming actually refers to a family of workshop formats, which allow for collaborative exploration and modelling of complex business domains."

## Big Picture EventStorming Process
The Big Picture format involves "a larger group of people (usually 10-15, but sometimes up to 30 people), who collaboratively explore everything that happens within a line of business by creating a timeline of events out of sticky notes on an 'infinite' modeling area (usually a very long wall)."

## Identifying Bounded Contexts
Through this workshop approach, teams discover "Bounded Contexts" together with developers—these represent "Units of homogenous language and model consistency, which together form a heterogeneous whole."

## Ubiquitous Language
Within each bounded context, participants establish "a Ubiquitous Language, where every term has exactly one, and only one, meaning." This precision prevents costly compromises across system design.

## Strategic Domain Discovery
An important outcome involves identifying "the core domain, and identify 'bottleneck' candidates, whose improvement might significantly benefit the whole system."

## Important Caveat
Notably, "The result of a Big Picture EventStorming workshop is a large map of the group's understanding of the business at the time of the modeling, never a final result."

## Core Team Types

The Team Topologies framework organizes people around four fundamental team topologies: stream-aligned, complicated subsystem, platform, and enabling teams.

## Stream-Aligned Teams

Stream-aligned teams are the principal team shape and are similar to feature teams but can have broader application than features, such as alignment to a product, a user journey or a persona. They can be aligned to a stream of work that is not necessarily a product.

## Cognitive Load Focus

Teams should be designed with cognitive load in mind, which means that they should be structured to minimise the cognitive load on individual team members. There is a natural limit to the number of responsibilities and domains a team can work across before they are "spread too thin" and delivery suffers.

## Platform and Supporting Teams

Platform teams enable stream-aligned teams to deliver work with substantial autonomy, by providing internal services to reduce cognitive load on stream-aligned teams to develop these underlying services.

## Core Principles

Pais & Skelton advocate for the 'inverse Conway maneuver' — structuring teams to achieve the desired architecture.

# Business-Capability Centric Teams: Key Concepts

## Definition
A business-capability centric team is one whose work aligns long-term to a specific business area. As defined in the article: "The team lives as long as the said business-capability is relevant to the business."

## Contrast with Project Teams
The fundamental difference is temporal: "This is in contrast to project teams that only last as long as it takes to deliver project scope." Project-centric models focus on delivering scope and handing off, while capability-centric teams "think-it, build-it and run-it" with end-to-end ownership.

## Cross-Capability Features
When initiatives span multiple capabilities—like an e-commerce checkout experience—the article notes these "might need a team of their own (or two teams, one for mobile and one for the laptop)." These cross-capability systems represent a deliberate exception to standard capability ownership.

## Conway's Law Relationship
The article addresses concerns directly: "But Conway's law isn't against a single team being responsible for multiple related components. It allows for high cohesion of component ownership and low coupling between teams and thus makes for better responsiveness."

The bounded context concept isn't explicitly mentioned, though the principle of drawing cohesive ownership boundaries aligns with that Domain-Driven Design pattern.

"A rule of thumb is to aim for two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work."

Product-mode teams require autonomy to "evolve their systems relatively independent of other teams" while maintaining alignment with enterprise architecture boundaries to prevent silos and dependencies.

Teams should be organized around partitions of "the long-term customer journey" with "each partition is customer-centric and is a meaty slice with data and business logic distributed across multiple systems."

# Notes-3 — SQ3: features crossing Bounded Contexts; product-level requests → context-owning teams

Gathered 2026-08-26 via WebFetch/WebSearch. Status per source: **opened in full** (tool returned page body and quotes were checked against it), **partial** (tool returned extracted quotes only; page body not seen whole), **could not be opened**. Quotes are verbatim as returned by the fetch tool; where the tool paraphrased I say so and do not quote. Nothing below is from memory.

---

## A. DDD sources

### A1. Evans, *DDD Reference* (2015) — https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf
Status: **partial** (direct fetch 403; opened via r.jina.ai, pattern text returned verbatim).
- Bounded Context: "Explicitly define the context within which a model applies. Explicitly set boundaries in terms of team organization, usage within specific parts of the application, and physical manifestations such as code bases and database schemas."
- Context Map: "Identify each model in play on the project and define its bounded context. Name each bounded context, and make the names part of the ubiquitous language. Describe the points of contact between the models, outlining explicit translation for any communication."
- Partnership: "Where development failure in either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both, forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts. Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and joint management of integration."
- Customer/Supplier Development: "Establish a clear customer/supplier relationship between the two teams, meaning downstream priorities factor into upstream planning. Negotiate and budget tasks for downstream requirements so that everyone understands the commitment and schedule."
- Conformist: "Eliminate the complexity of translation between bounded contexts by slavishly adhering to the model of the upstream team."
- Anticorruption Layer: "As a downstream client, create an isolating layer to provide your system with functionality of the upstream system in terms of your own domain model."
- Open-host Service: "Define a protocol that gives access to your subsystem as a set of services. Open the protocol so that all who need to integrate with you can use it. Enhance and expand the protocol to handle new integration requirements."
- Published Language: "Use a well-documented shared language that can express the necessary domain information as a common medium of communication, translating as necessary into and out of that language."
- Separate Ways: "Declare a bounded context to have no connection to the others at all, allowing developers to find simple, specialized solutions within this small scope."
- Big Ball of Mud: "Draw a boundary around the entire mess and designate it a big ball of mud. Do not try to apply sophisticated modeling within this context."
Relevance: Evans' unit for cross-context work is the *relationship between the two teams* (Partnership / Customer-Supplier), planned and budgeted as such — not a feature artifact. A feature spanning contexts is handled as coordinated planning under a named context-map relationship. No "feature" pattern exists in the Reference.

### A2. Fowler, bliki "BoundedContext" (2014) — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BoundedContext.html
Status: **opened in full**.
- "Bounded Context is a central pattern in Domain-Driven Design."
- "total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective"
- "Bounded Contexts have both unrelated concepts (such as a support ticket only existing in a customer support context) but also share concepts (such as products and customers)."
- "Different contexts may have completely different models of common concepts with mechanisms to map between these polysemic concepts for integration."
- "Usually the dominant one is human culture, since models act as Ubiquitous Language, you need a different model when the language changes."
- "DDD's strategic design goes on to describe a variety of ways that you have relationships between Bounded Contexts. It's usually worthwhile to depict these using a context map."
Relevance: contexts are partitions of *model and team*, not of features; shared concepts (customer, product) appear in several contexts by design, so a product-level feature touching "customer" will necessarily touch several.

### A3. Vernon, InfoQ report "Microservices and DDD" (2016) — https://www.infoq.com/news/2016/07/microservices-ddd-vernon
Status: **partial** (extracted quotes; secondhand report of Vernon's talk/writing).
- "one service per bounded context"; "one service and one bounded context should be one deployable unit"
- "modelling microservices in a bounded context determined in size by the ubiquitous language"
- "publishing the events for eventual use of other microservices"
- "With experience though, they may become more fine granular, creating more microservices and deployable units"
Relevance: cross-context coordination is via published domain events; the context, not the feature, is the deployable/owned unit.

### A4. Vernon, *IDDD* ch.14 (O'Reilly excerpt) — https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/implementing-domain-driven-design/9780133039900/ch14lev1sec2.html
Status: **could not be opened** (403 direct and via r.jina.ai). Not cited.

### A5. Microsoft p&p, *CQRS Journey* "Reference 6: A Saga on Sagas" (2012–14) — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/msp-n-p/jj591569(v=pandp.10)
Status: **opened in full**.
- "The term saga is commonly used in discussions of CQRS to refer to a piece of code that coordinates and routes messages between bounded contexts and aggregates. However, for the purposes of this guidance we prefer to use the term process manager to refer to this type of code artifact."
- "Typically, commands are sent within a bounded context. Events may have subscribers in the same bounded context as where they are published, or in other bounded contexts."
- "In a complex system that you have modeled using aggregates and bounded contexts, there may be some business processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in multiple bounded contexts. In these business processes multiple messages of different types are exchanged by the participating aggregates."
- "Secondly, the definition of the message flow is now located in a single place, the process manager, rather than being scattered throughout the aggregates."
- "It's important to note that the process manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes messages, and in some cases translates between message types."
- "Typically, you would expect to see a process manager routing messages between aggregates within a bounded context, and you would expect to see a saga managing a long-running business process that spans multiple bounded contexts."
Relevance: the technical answer to "a feature crosses contexts" is a named cross-context *process* (saga) with the flow defined in one place; each context still owns its own logic. This is the code-level analogue of a product-level artifact that names the whole flow and points to the contexts it touches.

### A6. Brandolini (reported), codecentric workshop review "EventStorming meets DDD" — https://www.codecentric.de/en/knowledge-hub/blog/eventstorming-meets-domain-driven-design-with-alberto-brandolini
Status: **partial** (secondhand workshop report; extracted quotes).
- Big Picture: "a larger group of people (usually 10-15, but sometimes up to 30 people), who collaboratively explore everything that happens within a line of business by creating a timeline of events out of sticky notes on an 'infinite' modeling area"
- Bounded contexts discovered as "Units of homogenous language and model consistency, which together form a heterogeneous whole."
- "a Ubiquitous Language, where every term has exactly one, and only one, meaning."
- Outcome includes identifying "the core domain, and identify 'bottleneck' candidates, whose improvement might significantly benefit the whole system."
- "The result of a Big Picture EventStorming workshop is a large map of the group's understanding of the business at the time of the modeling, never a final result."
Relevance: Big Picture is the product-level (whole-business timeline) view from which contexts are *derived*; the timeline (end-to-end flow) is the primary artifact and contexts are cut from it — the reverse of starting from contexts.

### A7. Brandolini, heuristic "Design Bounded Contexts around EventStorming Policies" (Virtual DDD) — https://virtualddd.com/heuristics/design-bounded-contexts-around-eventstorming-policies/
Status: **opened in full** (short page).
- "From a process or design level EventStorming, design your bounded contexts around the purple sticky called a policy."
- Examples given (tool paraphrase, not quoted): a "Reservation process policy" triggered when customers initiate bookings; long-running processes such as reservation-cancellation timers can be contained within a single bounded context.
Relevance: a context boundary is set around a *decision rule* (policy), not around a user-facing feature.

### A8. Nick Tune, "Aligning Teams with Business Capabilities to Improve Flow… Why You Shouldn't" — https://medium.com/nick-tune-tech-strategy-blog/aligning-teams-with-business-capabilities-to-improve-flow-why-you-shouldnt-b2996b959546
Status: **partial** (medium 403 direct; opened via r.jina.ai, extracted quotes).
- "Business capabilities are a structural decomposition of an organisation."
- "By identifying related concepts as bounded contexts, you are more likely to own things that change together, thereby increasing flow within each context."
- "The goal of autonomous contexts is to maximise flow — to find things which change together in software, group them as a code repository or software system, and ensure they are owned by a single autonomous team"
- "When we align teams with capabilities…we can make changes to a full slice of the application — from frontend UI to database, without requiring dependencies on another team."
- "Conversely, when there are changes to the user journey, multiple business capability teams may need to coordinate."
- "Flow is more akin to traffic lights — reducing flow in one direction to improve flow in another."
Relevance: explicit statement that *some* features (journey changes) will always cross context-owning teams; boundaries are a trade of which changes are cheap.

### A9. Nick Tune, "Confusing Process Stages With Bounded Contexts" — https://medium.com/nick-tune-tech-strategy-blog/confusing-process-stages-with-bounded-contexts-7cbba2dd069d
Status: **partial** (via r.jina.ai; extracted quotes).
- "you can't achieve these ideals if your organisational and technical boundaries constrain teams to work together on delivering almost every new idea"
- "every time a change is made in the Resubmit or Renegotiate service, a corresponding change has to be made in the case management system"
- "Collectively they should form a bounded context. A grouping of concepts that change together for business reasons"
- "The dashboard does not belong to the Review system — it's a composite of capabilities provided by other bounded contexts"
- "constant meetings, corresponding changes between one or more systems, and teams constantly being blocked by others are serious warning signs"
- "no organisation I've worked for got their boundaries right first time, and no-one I have ever worked with had a secret recipe"
Relevance: user-facing composites (dashboards, journeys) are *not* contexts; they compose capabilities from several contexts. A feature named at product level is often such a composite. Warning-sign list = measurable signal that decomposition is wrong.

### A10. Michael Plöd (INNOQ), "Identification of Team Boundaries" (2024) — https://www.innoq.com/en/articles/2024/07/identifikation-von-team-grenzen/
Status: **partial** (extracted quotes; author confirmed Michael Plöd).
- "A fracture plane is a natural seam in the software system that allows the system to be easily split into two or more parts." (quoting Team Topologies)
- "Bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying boundaries for teams in the team topology environment."
- A bounded context is "a boundary around a (technical) model that is expressed in a consistent language and tailored to a specific purpose."
- "Team Topologies explicitly stipulates a combination of fracture planes and encourages observing the section of a team from the perspective of different fracture planes."
- "A pivotal event lies at the boundary of a bounded context (or a subdomain)"; "swimlanes can be drivers for splitting bounded context candidates."
- "You should proceed cautiously and avoid a complete reorganization every quarter"
Relevance: contexts → team boundaries is the stated preferred mapping; boundaries are expected to be revised, but slowly.

### A11. INNOQ/Team Topologies minibook "Finding Software Boundaries for Fast Flow" — https://www.innoq.com/en/links/mini-book-ddd-tt/ (download: https://landing.teamtopologies.com/mini-book-ddd-tt)
Status: **partial** (landing page only; minibook itself not opened).
- "Domain boundaries and organizational dynamics are key to achieving these goals. Two approaches that are proven to deliver them are Team Topologies and Domain-Driven Design."
- Contributing authors listed: Susanne Kaiser, Alberto Brandolini, Nick Tune, Rich Allen, Matthew Skelton, Michael Plöd.
Relevance: evidence that DDD authors and TT authors jointly treat context = team boundary as the modern consensus. Content not read.

---

## B. Team / architecture practice

### B1. Team Topologies, "Key concepts" — https://teamtopologies.com/key-concepts
Status: **opened in full**.
- Stream-aligned team: "aligned to a flow of work from (usually) a segment of the business domain"
- Platform team: "a grouping of other team types that provide a compelling internal product to accelerate delivery by Stream-aligned teams"
- Enabling team: "helps a Stream-aligned team to overcome obstacles. Also detects missing capabilities."
- Complicated Subsystem team: "where significant mathematics/calculation/technical expertise is needed"
- Interaction modes — Collaboration: "working together for a defined period of time to discover new things (APIs, practices, technologies, etc.)"; X-as-a-Service: "one team provides and one team consumes something 'as a Service'"; Facilitation: "one team helps and mentors another team"
- "Stream-aligned teams own an entire slice of the business domain...end-to-end. The Stream-aligned teams are 'You Built It, You Run It' teams."
Relevance: cross-team work is handled by a *named interaction mode*, time-boxed (Collaboration) or contractual (X-as-a-Service) — TT's analogue of Evans' context-map relationships.

### B2. Team Topologies, "What are the core team types" — https://teamtopologies.com/key-concepts-content/what-are-the-core-team-types-in-team-topologies
Status: **opened in full** (page is a video transcript, not written definitions).
- "a stream-aligned team which other people call a product team - but they can be aligned to a stream of work that is not necessarily a product."
- Enabling teams: "typically teams of experts in a specific area that will collaborate with stream-aligned teams to help them gain the capabilities that they are missing."
- Platform: "they see other development teams as their customers effectively."
Note: the commonly quoted written definition ("aligned to a single, valuable stream of work… without requiring hand-offs to other teams") did NOT appear on the pages I opened; it surfaced only in search snippets (unopened). Treat as knowledge-only/unverified.

### B3. IT Revolution, "The Four Team Types from Team Topologies" (Skelton & Pais excerpt) — https://itrevolution.com/articles/four-team-types/
Status: **opened in full**.
- "A 'stream' is the continuous flow of work aligned to a single business domain or org capability."
- "This team is empowered to build and deliver value quickly, safely, and (this is key) independently. There shouldn't be any hand-offs to other teams to complete parts of the work."
Relevance: the ideal is *no* cross-team hand-off per stream; TT's answer to cross-context features is to align the team to the stream (journey/product) so the feature does not cross teams — the opposite move to "one team per context".

### B4. Fowler (Sriram Narayan), "Products Over Projects" (2018) — https://martinfowler.com/articles/products-over-projects.html
Status: **opened in full**.
- "Teams are funded to work on a particular business problem or offering over a period of time; with the nature work being defined by a business problem to address rather than a set of functions to deliver."
- Product-mode funds "building, running and iterating on the solution or even pivoting to a different solution till the underlying problem is verifiably solved."
- "Products-mode works best when teams are organized to be simultaneously aligned with business relevant capabilities and with enterprise architecture boundaries."
- Team partitions follow "the long-term customer journey" and "each partition is customer-centric and is a meaty slice with data and business logic distributed across multiple systems."
- "For initiatives that cut across multiple product-mode teams, it is recommended to appoint silo-penetrating, priority-negotiating, dependency-managing solution champions who work with product owners and business stakeholders."
- "Roadmap items are prioritized by product owners and their business counterparts. Cross-cutting initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership. Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to pre-existing product-mode teams."
- "A rule of thumb is to aim for two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work."
Relevance: the most explicit prescription found: a cross-team feature is an **initiative**, prioritised above the teams, owned by a named champion, parceled to existing teams, and capacity-capped. Requests go to a *team's roadmap* when contained, to *leadership* when cross-cutting.

### B5. Fowler bliki, "Business Capability Centric" (2022) — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BusinessCapabilityCentric.html
Status: **partial** (extracted quotes).
- "The team lives as long as the said business-capability is relevant to the business."
- "This is in contrast to project teams that only last as long as it takes to deliver project scope."
- Cross-capability systems such as an e-commerce checkout "might need a team of their own (or two teams, one for mobile and one for the laptop)."
- "But Conway's law isn't against a single team being responsible for multiple related components. It allows for high cohesion of component ownership and low coupling between teams and thus makes for better responsiveness."
Relevance: a recurring cross-capability feature (checkout) can become its *own* owned thing rather than staying a coordination problem.

### B6. Sam Newman, InfoQ podcast "Information Hiding, Ubiquitous Language, UI Decomposition" — https://www.infoq.com/podcasts/sam-newman-ddd-microservices/
Status: **partial** (transcript extracts).
- "A bounded context is effectively a way of us modeling these kinds of groups of functionality within a domain model so from the outside the bounded contexts allows you to kind of access some sort of higher level concepts"
- "Once they have an expectation about how that function works about the presence of that piece of data, that then makes it harder for you to change your microservice without breaking them."
- "If you have a series of webpages each page can be served up from different microservices, it's a very easy decompositional look because then you're effectively using URL routing as a way of dispatching requests"
- "If I now own delivery of an entrance slice of customer functionality inside my team then I can go a lot faster."
- "Looking at where your boundaries of your architecture without looking at the boundaries of your organization would be a bit crazy."
Relevance: UI decomposition (page/route per context) as the way a product-level feature is split so each piece lands in one context.

### B7. Sam Newman, "Microservices For Greenfield?" (2015) — https://samnewman.io/blog/2015/04/07/microservices-for-greenfield/
Status: **opened in full**.
- "Getting service boundaries wrong can be expensive. It can lead to a larger number of cross-service changes, overly coupled components."
- "Despite knowing the domain of continuous integration really well, their initial stab at coming up with service boundaries wasn't quite right."
- "This led to a high cost of change and high cost of ownership. After several months fighting this problem, the team decided to merge the services back into one big application."
Relevance: frequency of cross-context features is itself the metric for boundary quality; high frequency → merge or re-cut, not more coordination.

### B8. LeSS, "Feature Teams" — https://less.works/less/structure/feature-teams
Status: **opened in full**.
- "A feature team is a long-lived, cross-functional, cross-component team that completes many end-to-end customer features—one by one."
- Feature teams "work on a complete customer-centric feature, across all components and disciplines (analysis, programming, testing, …)"
- Component teams are "responsible for only part of a customer-centric feature," feature teams "responsible for complete customer-centric feature."
- Component teams: "dependencies between teams" leading to "additional planning"; feature teams "minimize dependencies between teams."
- Component teams "results in 'waterfall' development"; feature teams "support iterative development."
- "Hybrid models have the drawbacks from both worlds and can be…painful."
Relevance: the direct contrast point. LeSS treats a context-owning team as a component team and says the feature, not the component, is the unit of ownership. (Conflicts with Evans/Plöd/Vernon "one team per context".)

### B9. LeSS, "Product Backlog" — https://less.works/less/framework/product-backlog
Status: **opened in full**.
- "Multiple teams building a single product work from a single Product Backlog that defines all of the items/work to be done on the product."
- "Teams do not each have their own Product Backlog. Product Backlog Items are not pre-assigned to the teams."
- "Everything the teams work on should be visible on the Product Backlog."
- "finer grained items at the top and coarser grained items further down."
Relevance: "requests are made against a product" in its purest form — one product backlog, items unassigned until sprint planning. Our per-context brief is the opposite (pre-assigned).

### B10. Jeremiah Lee (ex-Spotify PM), "Spotify's Failed #SquadGoals" (2020) — https://www.jeremiahlee.com/posts/failed-squad-goals/
Status: **opened in full** (via r.jina.ai).
- "Autonomy requires alignment. Company priorities must be defined by leadership. Autonomy does not mean teams get to do whatever they want."

- "The parts on alignment and accountability were never completed."
Relevance: practitioner post-mortem — the failure mode of autonomous context/product teams is precisely the undefined cross-team feature process.

### B11. Spotify Engineering, "Spotify Engineering Culture part 1" (2014) — https://engineering.atspotify.com/2014/03/spotify-engineering-culture-part-1
Status: **opened** but page is a video wrapper; only text: "there's a lot of variation from squad to squad". Not usable for quotes.

Gathered 2026-08-26 via WebFetch/WebSearch. ## A. DDD sources

### A1. Evans, *DDD Reference* (2015) — https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf
Status: **partial** (direct fetch 403; opened via r.jina.ai, pattern text returned verbatim).
- Bounded Context: "Explicitly define the context within which a model applies. Explicitly set boundaries in terms of team organization, usage within specific parts of the application, and physical manifestations such as code bases and database schemas."
- Context Map: "Identify each model in play on the project and define its bounded context. Name each bounded context, and make the names part of the ubiquitous language. Describe the points of contact between the models, outlining explicit translation for any communication."
- Partnership: "Where development failure in either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both, forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts. Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and joint management of integration."
- Customer/Supplier Development: "Establish a clear customer/supplier relationship between the two teams, meaning downstream priorities factor into upstream planning. Negotiate and budget tasks for downstream requirements so that everyone understands the commitment and schedule."
- Conformist: "Eliminate the complexity of translation between bounded contexts by slavishly adhering to the model of the upstream team."
- Anticorruption Layer: "As a downstream client, create an isolating layer to provide your system with functionality of the upstream system in terms of your own domain model."
- Open-host Service: "Define a protocol that gives access to your subsystem as a set of services. Open the protocol so that all who need to integrate with you can use it. Enhance and expand the protocol to handle new integration requirements."
- Published Language: "Use a well-documented shared language that can express the necessary domain information as a common medium of communication, translating as necessary into and out of that language."
- Separate Ways: "Declare a bounded context to have no connection to the others at all, allowing developers to find simple, specialized solutions within this small scope."
- Big Ball of Mud: "Draw a boundary around the entire mess and designate it a big ball of mud. Do not try to apply sophisticated modeling within this context."
Relevance: Evans' unit for cross-context work is the *relationship between the two teams* (Partnership / Customer-Supplier), planned and budgeted as such — not a feature artifact. No "feature" pattern exists in the Reference.

### A2. Fowler, bliki "BoundedContext" (2014) — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BoundedContext.html
Status: **opened in full**.
- "Bounded Context is a central pattern in Domain-Driven Design."
- "total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective"
- "Bounded Contexts have both unrelated concepts (such as a support ticket only existing in a customer support context) but also share concepts (such as products and customers)."
- "Different contexts may have completely different models of common concepts with mechanisms to map between these polysemic concepts for integration."
- "Usually the dominant one is human culture, since models act as Ubiquitous Language, you need a different model when the language changes."
- "DDD's strategic design goes on to describe a variety of ways that you have relationships between Bounded Contexts. It's usually worthwhile to depict these using a context map."
Relevance: contexts partition *model and team*, not features; shared concepts (customer, product) appear in several contexts by design, so a product-level feature touching "customer" will necessarily touch several.

### A3. Vernon, InfoQ report "Microservices and DDD" (2016) — https://www.infoq.com/news/2016/07/microservices-ddd-vernon
Status: **partial** (extracted quotes; secondhand report of Vernon's talk/writing).
- "one service per bounded context"; "one service and one bounded context should be one deployable unit"
- "modelling microservices in a bounded context determined in size by the ubiquitous language"
- "publishing the events for eventual use of other microservices"
- "With experience though, they may become more fine granular, creating more microservices and deployable units"
Relevance: cross-context coordination via published domain events; the context, not the feature, is the owned unit.

### A4. Vernon, *IDDD* ch.14 (O'Reilly excerpt) — https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/implementing-domain-driven-design/9780133039900/ch14lev1sec2.html
Status: **could not be opened** (403 direct and via r.jina.ai). Not cited.

Status: **opened in full**.

- Contributing authors: Susanne Kaiser, Alberto Brandolini, Nick Tune, Rich Allen, Matthew Skelton, Michael Plöd.
Relevance: DDD and TT authors jointly treat context = team boundary as the modern consensus. Content not read.

- "Stream-aligned teams own an entire slice of the business domain...end-to-end. The Stream-aligned teams are 'You Built It, You Run It' teams."
Relevance: cross-team work handled by a *named interaction mode*, time-boxed (Collaboration) or contractual (X-as-a-Service) — TT's analogue of Evans' context-map relationships.

- "a stream-aligned team which other people call a product team - but they can be aligned to a stream of work that is not necessarily a product."
- Enabling teams: "typically teams of experts in a specific area that will collaborate with stream-aligned teams to help them gain the capabilities that they are missing."
- Platform: "they see other development teams as their customers effectively."
